thesis: Three UAA projects make the same move, learn what is normal for one particular thing and compare the real thing to it, and the stakes of getting it right climb from a ski turn to a senior's safety to a pipeline's heartbeat, while the reporting shows none of them proven yet.
supporting_facts: c1,c3: FlowLine grades a skier's own uploaded video because online feedback is generic
c5,c6: ANCHOR is designed to learn a senior's routines and alert family past a safety threshold
c7,c8,c9: a student models the compressor, the heartbeat of a proposed pipeline estimated over $54 billion
c10,c11: one first AI class in 2019 to a statewide symposium
counterpoint_to_honor: These are student and faculty showcase projects, so asking for proof is early. The film credits the capacity first, then says plainly that no users, accuracy figures, pilots or deployments are reported, all from one ADN feature, and asks what would prove each.
falsifiability: False if a primary source reports a pilot, accuracy figure or deployment (the 'unproven' claim expires), or if a project turns out to apply one fixed standard to everyone with no model of the particular subject.
second_movement: From idea to proof. Stakes rise across the three, then the film states the stage plainly and names what would count as proof: December launch, a first household for ANCHOR, a twin checked against a real compressor. Mike Jones ethics line (through 'right now') sits at the test.
valence: Earned optimism, hedged. The win is the people and direction of the work, not any proven product.

runner_up_angles.enthusiast: capacity pipeline from 2019 class to symposium (merged as the lineage beat)
runner_up_angles.skeptic: who answers when ANCHOR misses (merged as the stakes-rise question, asked not asserted)

debate: Explainer thesis kept as spine. Enthusiast supplies the lineage button. Skeptic supplies the rising-stakes ladder and the unproven stage, with no failure implied.
